en: *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (The Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only),
composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty.

The Śramaṇa Mingyu of Western Shu, together with the Bodhisattvas Huiyi, Hufa, and others, has composed this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* based on these thirty verses. Herein, I shall briefly set forth the reasons for doing so.
That is to say, within these thirty verses, the first twenty-four lines of verse clarify the characteristics of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-lakṣaṇa*);

the next line of verse clarifies the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-svabhāva*); and the final five lines of verse clarify the stages and positions of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra-gati-sthāna*). Regarding these twenty-four lines of verse:

The first one and a half lines briefly explain the characteristics of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). The subsequent twenty-two and a half lines extensively explain the characteristics of consciousness-only.
That is to say, an external interlocutor asks: "If there is only consciousness, why do the world and the various sacred teachings speak of a self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*)?"

Regarding Dharmapāla and the others: they are equal to Bandhuspāśa, Arciṣmān, Dharmamati, Sthiramati, Nanda, Vimalacandra, Jayabhadra, Dignāga, and Jñānacandra—these ten great masters who commented upon the *Triṃśikākārikā* and composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Therefore, by means of these verses, they have largely divided the work into three sections to reveal its outline, so that students may understand its essential points. Namely:
[The opponent] asks a question below to initiate the intent of the discourse:
"If there are only consciousnesses and all phenomena are non-existent, why do worldly people and the holy teachings commonly speak of a self and of phenomena?"
He replied by citing a verse. The verse says:
"Because of the provisional designation of self and phenomena, Various appearances arise. These depend upon what is transformed by consciousness;
This transforming [consciousness] is of only three kinds: Namely, the ripening, the deliberating, And the consciousness that discerns objects."

The first sentence answers the intent of the preceding question to clarify that the provisional designation of "self" (*ātman*) and "dharmas" (*dharma*) does not possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Since the interlocutor asks on the premise that self and dharmas exist substantially, the Bodhisattva refutes this by means of the three characters of "provisional designation. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"In both worldly convention and the holy teachings, it is said that there is a self and dharmas; however, these are merely established through provisional designation and do not possess a real nature. Regarding "self":

"Master" (*adhipati*) means one who exercises sovereignty; "dharma" means that which provides a model and maintains its own nature. "Master" implies the power of sovereignty, while "ruler" (*pati*) implies the power of decisive judgment;
since their meaning is identical to that of a "self" (*ātman*), they are collectively termed "master-self. "Model" (*naya*) refers to that which can produce understanding in sentient beings;

"maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to upholding its own intrinsic nature without abandoning it; since their meaning is identical to that of "dharma," they are collectively termed "model-dharma. As for the second phrase: [it means...]
Although my teaching is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), it nevertheless possesses the transformation of characteristics; thus it is said that "various characteristics undergo transformation.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Both of those possess the transformation of various characteristics.

The various characteristics of the self refer to sentient beings, living entities, and so forth, as well as stream-enterers, once-returners, and so forth. The various characteristics of phenomena refer to substance, qualities, actions, and so forth, as well as the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*)."

Regarding "realms" (*dhātu*) and so forth: "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) refers to the appearance of difference as designated in accordance with conditions. As for the phrase "my various [aspects]," it carries the sense of being a sovereign or master; this is possessed by both ordinary beings and sages.
Among ordinary beings, those who possess cognition are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*) or "living entities" (*jīva*); this term generally refers to the six classes of ordinary beings.

Those who have first destroyed delusions are called "stream-enterers" (*srotāpanna*); the "etc. includes all four types of noble ones (*ārya*). Regarding "the various aspects of phenomena" (*dharma*), it carries the sense of providing a standard or support; this applies to both internal and external [phenomena].

"All are pervasive" refers to the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) postulated by the Vaiśeṣikas. "Aggregates, bases, and elements" refers to the three divisions (*triskandha*) adhered to by other vehicles.
Regarding the phrase "provisionally established according to conditions": "provisional establishment" (*prajñapti*) means a conventional designation.

According to the condition of a sovereign, it is conventionally designated as the "self" (*ātman*); according to the condition of grasping and maintaining, it is conventionally designated as "dharmas. The third sentence refers to those...

The self and phenomena all depend upon the transformations of consciousness. A question in the treatise asks: "If these various characteristics are established through conventional designation (*prajñapti*), by what means are they accomplished?
The treatise further answers: "Those characteristics are all conventionally designated based upon the transformations of consciousness.
Through this dialogue in the treatise, it clarifies that the various characteristics of both the self and phenomena all depend upon consciousness.
Through transformation, various provisional designations are established; this is intended to refute their attachment to the notion that these exist substantially.
The fourth phrase means that those *ātman* and *dharmas* transformed by consciousness each have their own varieties, while this transforming consciousness [is singular].
Briefly summarized, there are three. The Treatise states: "Although the images manifested by consciousness are of immeasurable kinds, the types of the transforming consciousnesses are only three.

This means that although the transforming consciousnesses comprise the eight consciousnesses in total, as well as their associated mental factors (*caitta*), when their categories are classified, they fall into these three types.
Only three types are enumerated, termed the "three transformative consciousnesses. The fifth and sixth lines explain these three names. The treatise states:

"First is called *vipāka* (maturation), which is the eighth consciousness, because it is predominantly of a maturational nature. Second is called 'cognition' (*manana*), which is the seventh consciousness, because it constantly and thoroughly deliberates.
Third is called 'discernment' (*vijñapti*), which refers to the first six consciousnesses, because their discernment of objects is coarse."

Therefore, it is called "ripening" (*vipāka*) because it possesses three meanings: first, ripening through transformation, meaning that what was previously loathed becomes pleasing as the physical form undergoes change;
second, ripening at a different time, meaning the cause precedes and the result follows, rather than occurring simultaneously;

third, ripening as a different category, meaning that the nature of the former and the latter categories are distinct from one another. As for the phrase "constantly and thoroughly deliberating," it means "constantly..."

"Uninterrupted" means [the mind] is constant. "Discerning" refers to the grasping of a self. "Reflective" refers to the *manas*; because the *manas* reflects upon a self at every moment, it is so called.

Regarding the phrase "apprehending objects," this refers to the first six consciousnesses; as they take the five sensory objects as their domain, they all abide in the external gate, and are therefore said to have coarse characteristics.

Of the three categories mentioned, the former two each belong to a single consciousness, whereas the third category now comprehensively subsumes all six consciousnesses. Thus it is stated in the treatise.
It is said: "The classifications are only three.

Although the three names of the 'capable transformers' (*pariṇāma*) have already been briefly explained, their three characteristics have not yet been extensively analyzed. First, regarding the initial capable transformer:"
What are its characteristics?
Although the consciousnesses capable of transformation have already been listed by name, their specific meanings and characteristics have not yet been distinguished.

It is necessary to provide a detailed explanation in sequence before one can fully understand the distinctions between these three types of meaning; hence this question. First, [the text] below asks about the characteristics of the first transformative consciousness.
The initial ālayavijñāna, The maturation containing all seeds, Is unknowable; its appropriation and objective field are constant.
It is always associated with contact, Attention, feeling, perception, and volition, And is accompanied solely by the feeling of equanimity.
(The same applies to its contact and so forth, which are unobscured-neutral. It perpetually evolves like a violent torrent, And is relinquished at the stage of Arhatship.

This answers the preceding questions by clarifying the names, modes of activity (*ākāra*), associated mental factors (*caitta*), the three types of sensation, the four natures, the transformed and untransformed states, and the characteristics and meanings of the first transformative consciousness. The first two lines refer to the eighth consciousness, which has three names.
The first is *ālaya*, here translated as "storehouse" (*zàng*), because it possesses the three kinds of stores as its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The treatise states: The first transformative consciousness is termed *ālaya* in the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

This is because this consciousness possesses the meanings of being that which stores (*āśraya*), that which is stored (*āśrita*), and that which is clung to as a store (*upādāna*). Furthermore, it serves as a mutual condition for the defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa*), and sentient beings cling to it as their internal self.
This demonstrates the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the first transformative consciousness, which maintains the cause.

Because the fruit constitutes its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). When the treatise states, "Because this [ālayavijñāna] and the defilements (*saṃkleśa*) serve as mutual conditions," it explains the relationship between the container and the contained.
From the perspective of maintaining seeds, it is called the "container" (*āśraya*); from the perspective of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is called the "contained.

Furthermore, when it says, "Sentient beings grasp it as their internal self," it explains the meaning of being "grasped as a storehouse" (*upādāna*). This is because the seventh consciousness grasps it moment by moment.
Second, it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*) because it is the resultant characteristic produced by karma that brings about [rebirth]. The treatise states:
"This is the maturation fruit of the wholesome and unwholesome karma that draws forth birth within the various realms and destinies; therefore, it is termed 'maturation'.

This indicates the resultant characteristics of the first transformative consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Third, it is called "possessing all seeds," because it receives perfuming and maintains [them].

Because the seeds constitute its causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*). The treatise states: "Because it can grasp and maintain the seeds of all phenomena so that they are not lost, it is called 'all-seeds' (*sarvabījaka*).
This demonstrates the causal characteristic of the first transformative consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Regarding the verse’s statement, "Its objects, grasping, and location are unknowable," this means that the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of this consciousness as it perceives its objects is subtle and hidden; regarding the grasping (*upādāna*),...

Both [the object] and the location are difficult to understand. The treatise states: "Understanding" (*vijñapti*) means discernment (*vijñāna*); that is, the aspect of activity (*ākāra*), because consciousness has discernment as its aspect of activity.
"Location" (*sthāna*) means the locus; it is the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), for it is the locus upon which all sentient beings depend.
There are two kinds of appropriation (*upādāna*): namely, the various seeds and the body with sense organs. As for the various seeds, they refer to—

The various marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are called the habitual tendencies of conceptualization (*vikalpa-vāsanā*). Regarding "the body possessing faculties" (*sendriya-kāya*): this refers to the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and their physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Both of these are appropriated (*upātta*) by consciousness and grasped as its own substance (*svabhāva*), because they share the same security and peril.

Should it be asked: "The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that 'the seeds of the five consciousnesses are not included among those that are appropriated. Does this statement refer to the seeds or to the body possessing faculties?"

Regarding the two meanings of "simultaneously possessed" (*sahabhū-upātta*) and "appropriated" (*upātta*): how are they to be reconciled? The answer is: because there is a distinction between the seeds and the root-body as that which possesses appropriation.
With respect to "appropriation," there are two meanings: grasping [something] as one's own self and maintaining it so that it is not lost.

Regarding the eighth [consciousness] and its seeds, it takes only the sense of "maintaining" (dhāraṇa), not the sense of "encompassing" (saṃgraha), because it is neither an active manifestation (pravṛtti) nor a self-substance (svabhāva).

Regarding "feeling" (vedanā), it has two senses: "experiencing" (anubhava) and "causing awareness" (vijñapti). To experience means to take something as an object and cause the arising of awareness and feeling.

Regarding the eighth [consciousness] and its seeds, it takes only the sense of "experiencing," not the sense of "causing awareness," because it is not an active manifestation and lacks the capacity for awareness. This is...

Therefore, that treatise designates it as "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*) based on the two meanings of non-inclusion and non-cognition; whereas here, it is designated as "appropriated" (*upātta*) based on the two meanings of holding and experiencing.
Originally, these do not contradict one another. Furthermore, with respect to the root-body (*indriya-śarīra*), the eighth consciousness possesses all four meanings;
with respect to the seeds, it possesses only the two meanings of holding and experiencing; and with respect to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), it possesses only...

To take this as the object constitutes one meaning; there are no other three meanings. Regarding "it cannot be known": this refers to its mode of activity (*ākāra*), which is so extremely subtle that it is difficult to discern;
or else, it refers to the internal appropriated objects (*upātta-viṣaya*) that serve as its focal point (*ālambana*), which are likewise subtle.

The external vessel-world is called "unknowable" because its dimensions are difficult to measure. Regarding the phrase "the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of marks (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), and discrimination (*vikalpa*"):
"marks" refers to the objective aspect (*bhāga*), which is the object of perception; "names" refers to the subjective aspect (*bhāga*), which is the perceiving faculty.

Because these subject and object discriminations perfume and form karmic seeds, they are termed "habitual tendencies," which is synonymous with "seeds. Regarding the phrase "all material sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*")... [text continues]
The "roots" (*indriya*) are the ultimate roots (*paramārthendriya*); these are that which actually see and hear. The "bases" (*āśraya*) are the physical, sensory roots (*rūpīndriya*);

these are the forms of the eyes, ears, and so forth. Because the objects perceived by the eighth consciousness consist solely of the three factors of seeds, the body, and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), which are subtle and difficult to fathom, they are termed "unknowable.
The verse states: "It is always associated with touch, attention, feeling, and perception."
Regarding "associated with volition" (*manasikāra*): among the six categories of mental factors (*caitta*), this [volition] alone is present in every state. Thus, the treatise states:

"From beginningless time until it is transformed, the ālayavijñāna is at all times constantly associated with these five mental factors, because they are subsumed under the category of universal mental factors. That is to say, from beginningless time, this storehouse consciousness...

Come. Up to the eighth stage, it is called "the stage where the basis has not yet been transformed. Within the preceding seven stages, as well as the three stages of worthiness and the six paths of existence, these are termed "all positions.
In all these positions, [the mind] is constantly associated with these five mental factors; for by means of these five mental factors...

This is the meaning of "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*). Therefore, it co-exists with the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) throughout all states. The treatise states: "Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the differentiation of the transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three.
Its intrinsic nature is that which causes the mind and mental factors to contact their objects; its function is to serve as the basis for sensation, perception, volition, and so forth."
This refers to the mental factor of contact (*sparśa*). It arises from the transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three factors—the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.

Furthermore, its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is that which causes the mind and mental factors to come into contact with their objects. Its functional activity (*karma*) is that upon which feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth depend for their arising.
The treatise states: "Attention (*manasikāra*) has the nature of alerting the mind; it directs the mind toward the focal object."
Function (*karman*): It means that when the mind has not yet arisen, it arouses the mind; this is its essential nature (*svabhāva*). Once the mind has arisen, it leads it toward the object;
this is its functional activity (*kriyā*). The treatise states: "Feeling (*vedanā*) has the nature of experiencing the characteristics of objects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neutral.

Its function is to give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). That is to say, experiencing a favorable object is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); experiencing an unfavorable object is called painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*)."

That which takes as its object that which is neither [pleasant nor painful] is called equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). This is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of feeling (*vedanā*). Feeling serves as the basis for desire (*chanda*), and desire is itself craving (*tṛṣṇā*);

therefore, it is said that the arising of craving constitutes the functional activity (*karman*) of feeling. The treatise states: "Perception (*saṃjñā*) has the nature of grasping the image (*nimitta*) of an object;

its function is the establishment of various conventional expressions (*nāma-pada*). That is to say, by the power of perception, one grasps the image of an object—this is the essential nature of perception."

The establishment of names and conventions is the functional activity of perception (*saṃjñā*). The treatise states: "Volition (*cetanā*) has the nature of causing the mind to engage in formative activity;

its function is to employ the mind toward wholesome categories and so forth. That is to say, "formative activity" (*abhisamskāra*)—meaning deliberation and investigation—is the essential nature of volition.
They serve as the functional activity of volition (*cetanā*) for the mind and mental factors. The treatise states:

"Although these five—contact (*sparśa*) and the others—differ from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) in their modes of activity (*ākāra*), they are called 'associated' (*samprayukta*) because they share the same time, basis, and objective referent (*ālambana-vastu*). Regarding the difference in their modes of activity:

consciousness has the apprehension of objects as its mode of activity; contact has the causing of the mind to touch the object as its mode of activity; and attention (*manasikāra*)... [has the directing of the mind toward the object as its mode of activity].
Vigilance has the aspect of alerting the mind; feeling has the aspect of experiencing the object; perception has the aspect of grasping the image;
volition has the aspect of formative activity. Thus, they differ. However, their time, basis, and object are the same. Regarding the phrase "having an equal object":
it is called "associated" because of equality in terms of the entity, the location, the time, and the basis. The verse says "aspect."

It should be associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because it is devoid of suffering and pleasure. The two characters "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) are used interchangeably at the beginning and end of the verse.
The Commentary states: "The mode of activity (*ākāra*) of this consciousness is extremely indistinct; it cannot differentiate between the characteristics of adverse or favorable objects.

It proceeds as a subtle, uniform, and continuous stream. For this reason, it is associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity. That is to say, the feeling of equanimity is complete [in its neutrality]."

The five characteristics are identical in their mode of activity (*ākāra*) to those of the eighth consciousness; therefore, they are appropriately associated with it. First, it is not clearly manifest, because it lacks discernment (*mati*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Second, it does not engage in conceptual discrimination, as its objects are within the sphere of perception. Third, it is subtle, because its characteristics are not evident.
Fourth, it is of a single category, because it is neither subject to change nor easy to abandon. Fifth, it evolves as a continuous stream, because it is uninterrupted.
Regarding the verse’s statement that it is "unobscured and indeterminate" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*): among the four natures, it is of only one nature. The treatise states:

"This consciousness is exclusively comprised within the nature of unobscured-indeterminate maturation (*vipāka*). 'Obscured' (*nivṛta*) refers to defiled phenomena, because they obstruct the Noble Path and can also veil [the mind]."
It causes the mind to be impure; however, because it is not a defiled dharma, it is called "unobscured" (*anivṛta*).

It is "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because it does not possess the wholesome or unwholesome fruits of love or non-love, nor can its specific nature be definitively characterized as either wholesome or unwholesome.
Furthermore, because this eighth consciousness maintains the seeds of the untainted (*anāsrava*), it does not obstruct the Path. Moreover, it is the substratum of True Suchness (*tathatā*). And...
That which does not obscure the mind is called "unobscured" (*anivṛta*). That which is agreeable is the result of the wholesome; that which is disagreeable is the result of the unwholesome.
Because both are powerful and can be definitively distinguished, this consciousness lacks those [qualities] and is therefore called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).

When the verse states that "contact and the others are likewise," it is because the primary mind (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) share the same nature. The treatise says: "That is to say, just as the ālayavijñāna is..."

It is comprised within the category of the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). The same applies to contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*), because all associated mental factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*) must necessarily be of the same nature.
As for the statement in the verse that it "perpetually flows like a torrent," its essence is neither annihilated nor eternal; it is likened to a torrential stream.

The treatise states: "The term 'constant' (nitya) excludes interruption; 'transforming' (pariṇāma) indicates that it is not permanent. It is like a violent torrent; such is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of cause and effect.
Regarding the verse’s statement that one "abandons" at the stage of an Arhat, this refers only to abandoning the initial designation.

This is because the maturation (*vipāka*) and its seeds are abandoned last of all. The treatise further states: "When noble ones have severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and reached ultimate exhaustion, they are called Arhats."
At that time, because this consciousness is forever separated from the heavy burden (*dausthulya*) of afflictions, it is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).

As for the noble ones, when they first enter the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), their afflictions are not yet exhausted, and thus they are not called Arhats. Only upon reaching the stage where [afflictions] are completely exhausted do they receive this name.
"Arhat" translates here as "non-arising"; because afflictions no longer arise, one is named an Arhat. Coarse...
"Weighty" refers to the seeds. Because this consciousness contains the seeds of defilement and these are ultimately exhausted, it is described as "abandonment.
Thus has been explained the characteristic of the first transformation. What is the characteristic of the second transformation? The verse says:
Next, the second transformative consciousness is the consciousness named *manas*. It relies upon that [first consciousness] for its transformation and takes it as its object;

its nature and characteristic are reflection (*manana*). It is always accompanied by four afflictions—namely, self-delusion, self-view, self-pride, and self-love—as well as other factors such as contact;
it is subsumed under the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) category.
"Following its place of birth and its bondage, the Arhat’s meditative absorption of cessation, and the supramundane path—there is no [arising of this consciousness].

This question and answer clarifies the seventh [consciousness] in terms of its basis, objects, essence, function, associated mental factors, nature, realm, stage, and the characteristics of its state of relinquishment.
The first two lines of the verse explain the name of the seventh consciousness: *manas*, which here is translated as "mind."

Because it constantly and deliberatively cogitates, it is called "manas. The treatise says: Following the first transformation-consciousness, which is the result of maturation (*vipāka*), one should now explain the characteristics of the transformation-consciousness that consists of deliberative cogitation.
This consciousness is given a distinct name in the sacred teachings as *manas*, because its constant and deliberative cogitation is superior to that of the other consciousnesses.
That is to say, after the first transformative consciousness, it is logically necessary to proceed to explain the second transformative consciousness.

The characteristic of consciousness refers to the seventh consciousness, which is specifically termed *manas* in the sacred teachings because its functional activity of constant and thorough deliberation (*santatam parīkṣaṇam*) is superior to that of the other seven types of consciousness. The eighth consciousness is constant but not thorough; the sixth is thorough but not constant;
and the first five are neither constant nor thorough, as they are interrupted and non-conceptual. Only this seventh [consciousness] possesses both qualities.
It is both constant and continuous; therefore, it is superior to other consciousnesses. The verse says, "it evolves depending on that," which refers to its supporting faculty (*āśraya-indriya*).
This is because the seventh consciousness can only arise by depending upon the eighth consciousness. The Commentary states: "It evolves depending on that" reveals its support.

"That" refers to the aforementioned first transformative consciousness (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*), for the Sages have taught that this consciousness depends upon the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). [Verse]...

The phrase "taking that as its object" explains the objective referent (*ālambana*). This is because the seventh consciousness constantly takes the eighth consciousness as its object, grasping it as a self.
The treatise states: "That" refers to the aforementioned consciousness which serves as its support, for the Noble Ones teach that this consciousness takes the *ālaya-vijñāna* as its object.

As for the verse stating that its nature and characteristic consist of "cognition" (*manana*), this means that both the intrinsic nature of the seventh consciousness and its mode of apprehending objects are characterized by cognition.
Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists in deliberation (*manana*), it likewise employs that very [deliberation] as its mode of activity (*ākāra*).

By this, the specific name established for it is also explained: it is called *manas* because it is capable of discerning deliberation. Thus, by means of "deliberation," both its nature and its mode of activity are explained.
This also explains the nature and characteristics of the *manas*. Because both [the self-nature and the mental factors] involve deliberation (*samtīraṇa*), it is called *manas*.

Specifically, its self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is termed "deliberation as self-nature" (*svabhāva-saṃtīraṇa*), while its seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) is termed "deliberation as mental activity" (*ākāra-saṃtīraṇa*). The name *manas* also signifies deliberation.
Regarding the verse’s statement that it is "always accompanied by the four afflictions," this means it is always associated with the four fundamental afflictions.
The Commentary states: Here, the word "together" (*saha*) signifies the sense of association (*samprayoga*).

That is to say, from beginningless time until the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) has not yet occurred, this manas spontaneously and constantly takes the ālayavijñāna as its object and is associated with the four fundamental afflictions (*kleśa*). The verse says:

"Namely, self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), as well as self-pride (*ātma-māna*) and self-love (*ātma-sneha*)," which explains the names of these four afflictions. The Commentary states: Regarding "self-delusion":

This refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). Being deluded regarding the characteristic of a self and confused about the principle of non-self, it is called "self-delusion" (*ātma-moha*). This delusion is itself ignorance;
because one does not clearly comprehend that the essence of the eighth consciousness is fundamentally without a self, yet constantly clings to a self, it is termed self-delusion.
The treatise states: "Self-view" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) refers to self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*). It is so named because one falsely clings to what is not-self as being a self.
The view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). "View" is itself grasping (*parāmarśa*). Grasping means the sense of attachment and the sense of false appropriation.

Because that which is not-self is falsely appropriated as self, it is called the view of self. The treatise says: Self-conceit (*asmimāna*) refers to arrogance; it is the reliance upon the self that has been grasped.
It causes the mind to become uplifted; therefore, it is called *asmimāna* (self-conceit). *Māna* is arrogance; being haughty and self-important—this is the meaning of *māna*.
Because one relies upon a "self," the mind becomes uplifted by itself; this is termed *asmimāna*. The treatise says: "Self-love" (*ātmasneha*) refers to craving for the self.
Because one generates deep attachment toward the self that is grasped, it is called self-love. Love is indeed craving. Because...

Because one is greedily attached to the self and never relinquishes it, this is called "self-love" (*ātmasneha*). The verse states, "and those associated with other factors such as contact," which explains that it is associated with fourteen other mental factors (*caitta*).
"Other" refers to the eight great secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and discernment (*prajñā*) from among the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*);

the essential nature and functional activity of these nine mental factors will be explained in detail in the section on the third transformation (*tṛtīya-pariṇāma*). [The same applies to] contact and the others.

...as well as the other mental factors—feeling, perception, volition, and attention. The essential nature and functional activity of these five mental factors have already been explained in the section on the first transformation of consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
The Treatise says: However, there are eighteen mental factors associated with this [seventh] manas-consciousness:

namely, the nine previously mentioned factors, eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the discernment (*prajñā*) from among the object-specific factors (*viṣaya-nirūpaṇa*). There are no other mental factors, because they would be mutually contradictory. The verse states: "It is obscured (*nivṛta*)."

Regarding the inclusion by way of moral quality (*niyata-vyākaraṇa*): among the four types of moral quality, these are exclusively of the nature of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*). The treatise states:
"Because these four afflictions and so forth associated with this [manas] are defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), they obstruct the Noble Path and conceal one's own mind;

therefore, they are called 'obscured' (*nivṛta*). Since they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, they are termed 'unspecified' (*avyākṛta*). This refers to the four afflictions and their equivalents among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Because both are covered. Regarding "neither wholesome nor unwholesome": this means it is not wholesome and not unwholesome; it is designated as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The verse says, "bound to wherever it arises," which explains the realm and stage where the seventh consciousness resides.
That is to say, whichever realm the eighth consciousness arises in, the [seventh] is bound to that very realm. "Bound" (*baddha*) has the meaning of "not being separated from. This is because...

Because one clings to that eighth consciousness as the self at every moment. The treatise says: If the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) of a particular stage manifests before one, it is called "being born in that stage.
The afflicted manas (kliṣṭamanas) takes that as its object and clings to it as the self; thus, it is bound to it and is said to be "bound to that stage.
Regarding the verse’s statement that it does not exist for Arhats, in the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), or on the supramundane path: this means...
In these three states, there is no manas-consciousness: in the state of an Arhat, because one does not grasp at a self;

in the state of cessation, because active manifestations are suppressed; and in the supramundane path, because it is the initial turning of wisdom. For these reasons, in all three states, there is no manas. The treatise says:
"Arhat" generally indicates the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) for the three vehicles. In this stage, the defiled manas—

Because both the seeds and the active manifestations are permanently severed and extinguished, it is said that they do not exist. In the meditative attainment of cessation during the stage of training, both are temporarily suppressed and extinguished within the supramundane path; therefore, it is said that they do not exist.
Thus has the second transformative consciousness been explained. What are the characteristics of the third transformative consciousness? The verse says:
Next is the third transformative consciousness, Which is differentiated into six types. Its nature and characteristic consist in cognizing objects;
It is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral. These mental factors are pervasive, As well as those of specific objects, the wholesome, and the afflictions.

The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are indeterminate; all are associated with the three feelings (*vedanā*). First are the universal factors (*sarvatraga*), such as contact (*sparśa*) and the rest;

next are the object-specific factors (*viniyata*), namely: desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), which differ according to their respective objects.

The wholesome factors (*kuśala*) are: faith (*śraddhā*), shame (*hrī*), and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*); the three roots, beginning with non-attachment (*alobha*); diligence (*vīrya*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and heedfulness (*apramāda*).
Equanimity and non-harming; the afflictions are said to be greed, hatred, and delusion; pride, doubt, and wrong views.
The secondary afflictions are anger, resentment, concealment, vexation, envy, and avarice;
deception, guile, and harmfulness; arrogance, lack of shame, and lack of dread; restlessness and lethargy; lack of faith and indolence.
Laxity, loss of mindfulness, distraction, lack of clear comprehension, non-concentration, regret, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra—
each pair explained through question and answer—
clarify the third transformational consciousness: its mode of apprehending objects, the associated mental factors, and their nature and feeling.

The same applies to the subsequent meanings. Regarding the first two lines: the sixth consciousness necessarily shares with the preceding five [consciousnesses] the characteristic of perceiving coarse and manifest objects;

yet it possesses contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and birth (*jāti*), which are capable of bringing about future existence (*punarbhava*). Therefore, these six types are combined into a single "transforming" faculty. The treatise says:
Next, following the transforming consciousness of mental capacity (*manas*), one should explain the characteristics of the transforming consciousness that perceives objects. This consciousness...

There are six types of distinctions in total, as they differ according to the objects of the six sense faculties. Regarding the statement that "taking the apprehension of objects as their nature and characteristic":
because the first six consciousnesses take the apprehension of objects as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this very apprehension of objects constitutes their aspect (*ākāra*).

The treatise says: [This] simultaneously reveals both the intrinsic nature and the aspect of the six consciousnesses; since consciousness takes the apprehension of objects as its intrinsic nature, it is therefore...
Because it takes that as its mode of activity (*ākāra*), this also simultaneously explains the specific names established [for the three].

Since that which cognizes an object is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), the term "self-nature and mode of activity" refers to the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*); it is called "self-nature" because it cognizes itself, and each [of these] has a seeing division (*darśana-bhāga*), which is called the "mode of activity" because it cognizes objects.
This also simultaneously explains the specific names [of the three], for *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* are each distinct.

It is well known that the eighth [consciousness] is called *citta* (mind) because it accumulates; the seventh is called *manas* (intellect) because it deliberates; and the first six are called *vijñāna* (consciousness) because they cognize objects.

Thus, the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is explained by means of the cognition of objects. When the verse says "wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral," it means that these six consciousnesses possess all three moral natures.
The treatise states: These six evolving consciousnesses are associated with the eleven mental factors, such as faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth.
[The universal mental factors] are associated with those of a wholesome nature; they are not associated with the ten unwholesome factors, such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth;

and they are not associated with those of an indeterminate nature. The verse states that these mental factors are "universal, object-specific, wholesome, afflictive, secondary afflictions, and indeterminate," meaning they are present in all six classes of mental factors within the six consciousnesses. The treatise says: These six...
The evolving consciousnesses are universally associated with six categories of mental factors (*caitta*).
Although these mental factors do not differ in their names or essential meanings, they are distinguished by six categories of types:

namely, five universal factors (*sarvatraga*), five object-specific factors (*viniyata*), eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*), six root afflictions (*kleśa*), twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*). Such are the six categories.
Taken together, there are fifty-one [mental factors]. This is because they can definitely be found within all states of mind;

because they arise by taking various distinct objects as their conditions; because they can only arise within wholesome states of mind; because their nature is fundamental and is subsumed under the afflictions (*kleśa*);

because they are exclusively of the nature of the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the afflictions; and because they are indeterminate with respect to both the wholesome and the defiled. These six preceding phrases constitute the explanation.

The names and meanings of the six stages should be understood according to their respective order. When both the verse and the commentary state that [the mind] is associated with the mental factors of the six stages, the wording is general while the intended meaning is specific.
Here, the discussion proceeds by means of the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*), and thus the eight consciousnesses are divided into three;

this constitutes the general statement. However, when speaking in terms of the wisdom of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti-jñāna*), the eight consciousnesses are divided into four; therefore, the first five [consciousnesses] are distinguished separately.

The sixth [consciousness] constitutes two categories of mind; this is what is meant by "the distinction of the mental faculty" (*manas*). When it is said that these [mental factors] are generally associated with the six stages, this refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

If one relies on the preceding five [sensory consciousnesses], they possess only thirty-four mental concomitants (*caitta*), because the remaining seventeen mental concomitants are not associated with them.
When the verse states that "all are associated with the three feelings," this refers to the three feelings of the first six consciousnesses.

All [of these] are present. The *Śāstra* says: These six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are easily detached and unstable; therefore, they can all be associated with the three feelings (*vedanā*).
"Easily detached" means that they are subject to interruption and transformation. "Unstable" refers to their relation to suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.

Because they are not restricted to a single object. The verse states, "First, the universal [factors], contact and so forth," which explains the stage of the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). There are five such mental factors:

contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). The essential nature and functional activity of these five mental factors have already been explained in the section on the first transformation of consciousness.

The verse states, "Next, the object-specific [factors] are desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)," referring to those whose objects of focus are not...
Regarding the "common" [mental factors]: this explains that there are five mental factors (*caitta*) in the category of object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).
The treatise asks: What is desire (*chanda*)? Its nature is the aspiration for an object of enjoyment; its function is to serve as the basis for diligence (*vīrya*). What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?

Its nature is the confirmation and apprehension of a determined object; its function is to be unshakeable by others. What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)? It causes the mind to be clear regarding an object previously experienced...
Its nature is non-forgetfulness of what has been recorded; its function is to serve as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). What is concentration?
Its nature is to cause the mind to focus one-pointedly on the object of observation without distraction; its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom (*prajñā*).

What is wisdom? Its nature is the discernment of the object of observation; its function is to sever doubt. The verse states that "wholesome" refers to faith, shame, dread, and so forth—these four lines explain the wholesome.
There are eleven mental factors (caitta) in this category. The treatise says: Those that coexist exclusively with wholesome minds are called wholesome mental factors. What is faith (*śraddhā*)?

It is characterized by deep conviction, aspiration, and desire regarding reality, virtue, and capability; its intrinsic nature is the purification of the mind; its function is to counteract lack of faith and to delight in what is wholesome.
Regarding the terms "reality, virtue, and capability": "reality" refers to the actual principle of the true substance of all phenomena; "virtue" refers to the true [qualities] of the Three Jewels.

Purity of virtue (*śuddhaguṇa*). It is the capacity for the wholesome qualities of both the mundane and supramundane realms. Regarding the three aforementioned types [of wholesome states], profound acceptance, profound delight, and profound aspiration—these are called faith (*śraddhā*).
The treatise says: What is shame (*hrī*)? Its nature is to revere and honor the noble and the wholesome based on the power of oneself and the Dharma.
Its function is to counteract lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and to bring rest to unwholesome conduct. What is dread of blame (*apatrāpya*)? Based on the world...

Shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) has the nature of slighting and rejecting the violent and evil. Its function is to counteract the lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*) and to bring about the cessation of unwholesome conduct.

Regarding the phrase "non-attachment and so forth," "and so forth" includes non-hatred and non-delusion; these three are called roots because they are preeminent in producing wholesome states. The three unwholesome roots are as follows: [greed, hatred, and delusion].
Because it is the proximate antidote. What is non-attachment (*alobha*)? Its nature is non-attachment toward existence (*bhava*) and the requisites for existence (*bhavopakarana*).

Its function is to counteract attachment and to perform wholesome deeds. Regarding the phrase "existence and the requisites for existence": "existence" refers to the three realms of existence as the fruit, while "requisites for existence" refers to their causes.
Because one is without craving for either cause or fruit within the three realms, [it is called non-attachment]. The treatise asks: What is non-hatred (*adveṣa*)?

Its nature is the absence of malice toward suffering and the instruments of suffering; its function is to counteract hatred and to perform wholesome deeds. Regarding "suffering and the instruments of suffering":
suffering is the effect, while the instruments of suffering are the cause. Because there is no malice toward either the cause or the effect of suffering, the treatise states:

What is non-delusion (*amoha*)? Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is clear understanding regarding all principles and phenomena; its function (*karman*) is to counteract delusion and to perform wholesome deeds.
Delusion is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*); being obscured and confused regarding principles and phenomena is termed ignorance.

Now, when we speak of "non-delusion," it means the absence of ignorance, which is precisely the capacity for clear understanding—this constitutes its essential nature. The treatise states: "Diligence" refers to *vīrya* (exertion) regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome.

In the context of the factors to be cultivated through abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*), its intrinsic nature is vigor (*vīrya*). Its function is to counteract laziness (*kausīdya*) and to fulfill wholesome qualities. "Vigor" (*vīra*) signifies superior progress, thereby distinguishing it from all defiled phenomena;

"ardor" (*udagra*) signifies purity and refinement, thereby distinguishing it from the pure-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). This clearly demonstrates that diligence (*vīrya*) is comprised solely within the category of the wholesome.

The treatise states: "Tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*) refers to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); it is the removal of heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*), bringing the body and mind into a state of harmonious flexibility and functional capacity.
It has the nature of being the antidote to lethargy (*styāna*) and the function of transforming the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). As for heedfulness (*apramāda*):

it has the nature of diligence (*vīrya*), the three roots of goodness, and the prevention and cultivation regarding that which is to be practiced and abandoned; its function is to counteract negligence (*pramāda*) and to bring to completion all mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds.
That is to say, through the single factor of diligence and the three roots of goodness, regarding the evils to be abandoned, it prevents them...

Non-arising [of unwholesome states] and the cultivation of cultivated virtues so that they increase is called heedfulness (*apramāda*); it does not possess a separate substantial entity. The treatise asks:
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)? It is when vigor and the three roots cause the mind to abide in a state of evenness, rectitude, and effortlessness.
Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the antidote to restlessness (*auddhatya*). Its function (*karma*) is to abide in tranquility. What is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*)?
It consists in not causing injury or affliction to sentient beings. Its intrinsic nature is non-hatred (*adveṣa*). It can serve as the antidote to harming.

Its function is compassion (*anukampā*). The treatise says: Among these eleven factors, three are nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*), namely: heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and non-harming; their meanings are as previously explained. The remainder...

Eight [of these factors] exist substantially because their characteristics and functions are distinct. That is to say, the two dharmas of heedfulness (*apramāda*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) both have diligence (*vīrya*) and the three roots as their essence.
The single dharma of non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) has non-aversion (*adveṣa*) as its essence; therefore, they are said to be nominal. The verse says:
"Afflictions" refers to greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views. This explains the names of the six mental factors that constitute the root afflictions.
The treatise states: "Because these six—greed and the others—are by nature subsumed under the category of root afflictions, they receive the designation 'affliction'."
What is greed (*lobha*)? Its nature is attachment to existence and the requisites for existence;
its function is to obstruct non-greed and to give rise to suffering. What is hatred (*dveṣa*)? Its nature is malice toward suffering and the requisites for suffering;

its function is to obstruct non-hatred, to constitute a state of lack of peace, and to serve as the basis for unwholesome conduct. What is delusion (*moha*)? It is confusion and darkness regarding all principles and phenomena.
Its nature is that which can obstruct non-delusion. Its function is to serve as the basis for all defilements. What is pride?
Its nature is to exalt oneself in relation to others based on self-reliance. Its function is to obstruct non-pride and to give rise to suffering.
What is doubt? Its nature is hesitation regarding the principles of the Truths. Its function is to obstruct the wholesome qualities of non-doubt. What is wrong view?
It has the nature of defiled wisdom that erroneously investigates the principles of the truths;

its function is to obstruct right vision and to bring about suffering, for those with wrong views undergo much suffering. The verse states: "The secondary afflictions refer to the eight beginning with anger."

The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are explained as being twenty in number, divided into three categories: small, medium, and great. The treatise states: "These are exclusively distinctions within the states of the primary afflictions;
because they are of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), they are called secondary afflictions. These twenty types are further divided into three classes:

first, the ten beginning with anger (*krodha*), which are called "small secondary afflictions" because they arise individually; second, the two beginning with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), which are pervasive...

Because they are unwholesome, they are called the medium secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). The eight [afflictions] beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*) are called the universal secondary afflictions because they pervade all defiled minds.
What is anger (*krodha*)? It has the nature of a sudden outburst directed toward a presently perceived object that is disadvantageous;
its function is to obstruct the absence of anger and to lead to the grasping of weapons. What is resentment (*upanāha*)? Preceded by anger, it consists of harboring malice and refusing to let go.
Enmity has resentment as its nature; it functions to obstruct freedom from resentment and has the activity of causing burning affliction. What is concealment?

It has the hiding of one’s own committed transgressions as its nature, out of fear of losing profit and reputation; it functions to obstruct freedom from concealment and has the activity of causing regret and affliction. What is vexation?

Having anger and resentment as its precursor, it is characterized by a harsh and violent heat that pursues and contacts [the object]; it has perversity as its nature; it functions to obstruct freedom from vexation. *Kṣudh* (famine/hunger).

[The syllable] *śu* (or *kṣu*) constitutes its activity. What is envy (*īrṣyā*)? It has the nature of being envious and jealous, coveting one's own fame and profit while being unable to endure the prosperity of others.

Its activity is to obstruct non-envy and to produce grief and distress. What is avarice (*mātsarya*)? It has the nature of being secretive and stingy regarding wealth and the Dharma, being unable to give or relinquish them.
Its activity is to obstruct non-avarice and to produce base accumulation. What is deception (*māyā*)? It is for the sake of obtaining...
Flattery (*māyā*) has gain and fame as its cause; it is characterized by hypocrisy and deceit, and its function is to obstruct non-deception and to serve as a basis for wrong livelihood.
What is guile (*śāṭhya*)? It is the feigning of unusual behavior for the sake of deceiving others; it is characterized by crookedness and its function is to obstruct honest instruction.
What is harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*)? It is the absence of compassion toward sentient beings, characterized by the intent to injure and afflict them.

Its nature is that which can obstruct non-harming; its function is to cause affliction and distress. What is *mada* (intoxication/arrogance)? It is the deep arising of defiled attachment toward one’s own flourishing prosperity;
its nature is intoxicated pride; its function is to obstruct non-arrogance and to serve as a basis for defilement.

The above concludes the explanation of the minor derivative [afflictions]. The treatise asks: What is *āhrīkya* (lack of shame)? Its nature is to disregard one’s own dharma and to treat the virtuous and good with contempt and rejection; it can obstruct...

The hindrance of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) has the function of producing unwholesome conduct. What is lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*)? It has the nature of disregarding the world and honoring violence and evil;
it can obstruct dread of blame and has the function of producing unwholesome conduct. The above concludes the explanation according to the [Abhidharmakośa-]bhāṣya.
The Treatise says: What is restlessness (*auddhatya*)? Its nature is to cause the mind to be non-quiescent with respect to its object;
its function is to obstruct equanimity (*upekṣā*) and *śamatha*. What is lethargy (*styāna*)? Its nature is to cause the mind to be incapable of functioning with respect to its object;
its function is to obstruct pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and *vipaśyanā*. What is lack of faith (*āśraddhya*)? It is the lack of acceptance toward reality, virtue, and capability.
Lack of aspiration (*anabhilāṣa*) has defilement of mind as its intrinsic nature; its function is to obstruct pure faith and to serve as a basis for indolence. What is indolence (*kausīdya*)?
It has laziness regarding the cultivation of the wholesome and the abandonment of the unwholesome as its intrinsic nature; its function is to obstruct diligence and to increase affliction.
What is heedlessness (*pramāda*)? Its nature is to be unrestrained and dissolute, failing to guard against or cultivate the factors of defilement and purification.

Its function is to obstruct heedfulness and to serve as the basis for the increase of evil and the diminution of good. What is loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*)? Its nature is the inability to clearly remember various objects of focus.
It functions to obstruct right mindfulness and to serve as the basis for mental distraction (*vikṣepa*). What is distraction (*vikṣepa*)? Regarding...

The nature of all objects of perception (*ālambana*) is to cause the mind to wander; their function is to obstruct right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) and to serve as the basis for faulty wisdom (*kuprajñā*).
What is non-apprehension (*asamprajanya*)? Its nature is erroneous understanding regarding the object under observation; its function is to obstruct right knowledge and to lead to transgressions.
Among these twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the ten minor ones and the three major ones are certainly nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*); the remainder...
All of these are real. Regarding the "three great [unwholesome factors]," they are: heedlessness (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*).

The verse states: "The indeterminate are remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*); applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) each have two. This explains the four types of mental factors within the category of the indeterminate. The treatise says:

Remorse, sleep, applied thought, and sustained thought are all indeterminate with respect to the wholesome, the defiled, and so forth; they are not like contact (*sparśa*) and the others, which are necessarily universal.

Because they are mental factors, unlike desire and so forth, which are not necessarily universal across all stages, they are designated as "unstable. *Kaukṛtya* (remorse) refers to regretting an action performed poorly;
its intrinsic nature is subsequent regret, and its function is to obstruct *śamatha* (calm abiding). *Middha* (drowsiness) refers to sleep;

its intrinsic nature is a state of mental dullness and contraction that renders the body involuntary, and its function is to obstruct *vipaśyanā* (insight). *Vitarka* (applied thought) refers to seeking; it causes the mind to be hurried and restless toward the object of attention.

Regarding the term "object" (*viṣaya*): its nature is coarse mental activity. *Vicāra* (sustained thought) means investigation; its nature is subtle mental activity that causes the mind to be hurried with respect to the object of mental discourse (*manojalpa*).
Both of these have as their function the basis for states of physical and mental ease or unease.
The term "hurried" (*saṃtvaraṇa*) has the meaning of rapidity. The "object of mental discourse" refers to the object apprehended by the mind, because it mostly relies upon names and expressions.

Coarse activity refers to wandering through external objects and making shallow investigations into phenomena; subtle activity refers to moving briefly through external objects and making deep investigations into phenomena.
Thus, when body and mind are at peace, this is the meaning of subtle activity; when body and mind are not at peace, this is the meaning of coarse activity.
The Commentary says: The phrase "two of each" indicates two pairs. The first refers to regret (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*);
the second refers to vitarka and vicāra. These two pairs are distinct in their respective categories; therefore, the expression "one-two" indicates two sets of two.
As for the phrase "these two sets of two," it means that the aforementioned two [pairs] each consist of two types, namely: regret and sleep, as well as vitarka and vicāra.
The types are distinct. Furthermore, the text concludes by stating: "Therefore, the terms 'one' and 'two' manifest two pairs of types; that is, first, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*);

second, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). This is because each of these two [categories] consists of two types. The above is the explanation of the names. There is also an explanation of the meaning. The treatise says:
"Each of these has two [subdivisions], namely, defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*). They are not like the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the defiled, which each function as..."
Because they are one, the phrase "each of the two has two" is stated to clarify the meaning of their non-fixed nature; thus, the inclusion of this expression is profoundly useful.

By means of "each of the two has two," it explains both the names and the meanings, as well as distinguishes between those that are exclusively wholesome and those that are exclusively defiled; therefore, it is said to be profoundly useful.
Having explained the association of the six consciousnesses with mental factors (*caitta*), how should one understand their manifest states? The verse says:
Relying upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), The five consciousnesses appear according to conditions;
They may arise together or not, Just as waves depend upon water. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises constantly, Except when born in the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*).

And the two mindless attainments, sleep, and fainting—these questions and answers clarify the states in which the first six evolving consciousnesses manifest. This verse of eight lines has three distinct sections.
The first line concerns the "common support" of the six consciousnesses, as the six evolving consciousnesses share a common support in the eighth fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Therefore, the next three lines concern the gateway of the simultaneous operation of the five consciousnesses, because the first five consciousnesses are of a similar category.
The final four lines concern the gateway of the presence or absence of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), as it constantly arises except for five states. The Treatise says:
"The fundamental consciousness" refers to the *ādānavijñāna*, because it is the root from which all defiled and pure phenomena arise. "The support" refers to the preceding six [consciousnesses].

The evolving consciousnesses take the fundamental consciousness as their common and immediate support (*sahaja-āśraya*). *Ādāna* is translated here as "grasping" or "holding. Regarding the term "common and immediate support":
"common" refers to the six consciousnesses; "immediate" refers to the seeds; and "support" refers to the fundamental [consciousness]. This means that the six evolving consciousnesses...
The seeds and their actualization both depend upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

As for the five consciousnesses appearing according to conditions, this refers to the first five consciousnesses being induced by conditions such as attention (*manasikāra*), sense organs (*indriya*), and objects (*viṣaya*); "whether they arise together or not" refers to external conditions.
Because there are both sudden and gradual [arising]. If the power of the various conditions, such as the five sense objects, is equal, the five consciousnesses arise simultaneously;

if they are slightly unequal, they do not arise together. This is like waves depending upon water: water is a metaphor for the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and waves are a metaphor for the first five consciousnesses.
Depending on conditions such as wind and objects, more or fewer waves arise; the arising of the five consciousnesses is likewise. As for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)...

Regarding that which "constantly manifests": the treatise states, "The sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), is capable of its own deliberation and operates through both internal and external gates without depending on many conditions.
With the exception of five states, it is able to manifest constantly; therefore, the time it is interrupted is brief, while the time it manifests is extensive."
For this reason, it is not mentioned here. This [consciousness] manifests according to conditions, with the exception of three states where it does not arise:
first, the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*); second, the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); third, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);

fourth, the state of sleep; and fifth, the state of fainting. Within these five states, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not arise, because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the sixth consciousness...
The objects of perception can be known in all cases; however, within these five stages, they cannot be known at all because they lack mental aspects (*ākāra*).
Having extensively analyzed the characteristics of the three transformations, how should one understand that they serve as the basis for the two parts transformed by themselves?

Based on what is transformed by consciousness, "self" and "dharmas" are metaphorically designated; they do not exist as separate, real entities. For this reason, is it the case that all things are "consciousness-only"?

Having extensively explained [the preceding], he concludes by summarizing the three types of transformation as the basis for the two parts—the perceived and the perceiving—which are themselves transformed [by consciousness].
Regarding the phrase "How so? [the text] further asks: "My doctrine is not [of the nature of] substantial reality; there is only the meaning of consciousness-only.
The verse says:
"The transformations of these various consciousnesses Are the subject and object of discrimination; By virtue of this, both of them are non-existent."

Therefore, "all is consciousness-only" answers the intent of the preceding question by clarifying that the two divisions—the perceived (nimitta) and the perceiving (darśana)—as well as the real self and real dharmas grasped therein, are all non-existent;
thus, there is only consciousness. The first two phrases clarify the characteristics of the transforming subject and the transformed object, thereby establishing the capacity [of consciousness].

The object of apprehension (*grāhya*). The third phrase clarifies that both the internal and external are empty. The fourth phrase reveals the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). The treatise says:
"These various consciousnesses" refers to the three types of transformative consciousness previously mentioned, along with their associated mental factors (*caitta*).

All of these are capable of transforming themselves into the appearance of the two parts—the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*)—and thus are given the name "transformation. The transformed seeing-part is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), as it is the subject that apprehends.

Because it is a characteristic (*nimitta*), the transformed objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is called the "object of discrimination" (*vikalpya*), for it is that which is grasped by the seeing [aspect].

By this correct reasoning, those real selves and dharmas, apart from what is transformed by consciousness, are definitely non-existent; for, apart from the grasper and the grasped, there is no distinct characteristic.

There are no real entities, because they are devoid of the two characteristics. Therefore, all things—whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether real or provisional—are not separate from consciousness.
If there is only consciousness and no external objects at all, by what means do various conceptual discriminations arise? "If only...
introduces the Mahāyāna doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). "By what... is the interrogative phrase. That is to say:

if there is only consciousness and no objective realm, by what cause do various states of mind come into being? Since there is no object to draw the mind toward it, from what does the deluded mind arise?
[It] arises.
The verse says:
Through all modes of consciousness, it transforms in such and such ways by virtue of their mutual influence.

The various conceptualizations that arise answer the meaning of the preceding question by clarifying that all diverse conceptualizations are produced through the power of transformation of the *ālayavijñāna* (all-seed consciousness).
"By means of the all-seed consciousness" refers to all the seeds within consciousness.

It is capable of producing various types of discrimination. The eighth fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) contains and stores the seeds of the eight consciousnesses and their respective mental factors (caitta).
From these respective direct seeds, it transforms and gives rise to the various discriminating minds.

The phrase "transforming in such and such a manner" indicates that the seeds transform to produce the manifest activities (pravṛtti). This is just as, for example, visual consciousness arises from its own direct seed.

This transformation gives rise to the manifestation of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which is able to discern forms (*rūpa*), and so on up to tactile consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), which arises from its own immediate seeds.

Thus, this transformation gives rise to the manifestation of tactile consciousness, which is able to discern tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*). Since the five consciousnesses are thus, the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses are likewise.
Therefore, it is said: "Thus and thus it transforms. Regarding the phrase "by the power of successive succession," this refers to the eight [consciousnesses].
Consciousness, when arising from seeds, arises by means of mutual conditioning; therefore, it is called "mutually dependent power" (*anyonya-vaśa*).

Regarding "the various [types of] discrimination that arise," this refers to the eight kinds of consciousness and their associated mental factors (*caitta*), all of which are termed "discrimination"; hence the expression "various."
Although internal consciousness exists, there are no external conditions; by what means, then, does the cycle of birth and death continue for sentient beings?
The phrase "although [it exists]" below restates the correct principle of Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātra (Cognition-Only). The phrase "by what" below is an interrogative term. That is to say:
if there are no external conditions, the internal mind does not arise. Because the mind does not arise, karma itself is not produced. By what, then, do worldly sentient beings [continue]?
And thus there is the continuity of birth and death.
The verse says:
"Due to the habitual tendencies of various karmas, together with the habitual tendencies of the two graspings, once the previous maturation has been exhausted,"
Furthermore, regarding the arising of other maturations (*vipāka*), this answers the intent of the previous question by clarifying the continuity of birth and death.

This is also due to the harmonious convergence of equal forces between the seeds of karmic habituation within consciousness and the seeds of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-graha*). These enable sentient beings to manifest the characteristics of arising and ceasing. The first two lines clarify this.
The three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are as follows: the habitual tendencies of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*), which refers to all karmas;

and the two types of habitual tendencies of grasping (*upādāna-vāsanā*), namely the grasping of self-identity (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping of names and conventions (*nāma-kalpa*). These correspond to the latter two phrases [of the verse].

This means that sentient beings continue through birth and death (*saṃsāra*) due to these three habitual tendencies; what need is there for external conditions for birth and death to be established? Regarding the phrase "all karmas," it refers to [the first type of habitual tendency].

There are three types: namely, meritorious (*puṇya*), non-meritorious (*apuṇya*), and immovable (*āniñjya*). Because both their intrinsic nature and their results are desirable and their characteristics are preeminent, they are called meritorious karma.
Because both their intrinsic nature and their results are undesirable and their characteristics are base, they are called non-meritorious karma.
Because they possess a specific measure of karma, abide in one-pointedness of mind, and do not waver, they are called immovable karma.

It is also called neutral karma (*avyākṛta-karma*). This refers to the karma of the stages of the two higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); because these absorptions can cause the mind to abide in a single object, they are specifically termed "neutral.
Second, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the grasped are all included within the grasper. Regarding the phenomena that are grasped, there are four kinds:
first, grasping at signs and views; second, grasping at name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); third, grasping at the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); fourth, grasping at...
"Root and branch": the root refers to the collective retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*), while the branch refers to the individual retribution (*viśeṣa-vipāka*).

Those four aforementioned types of objects of apprehension (*grāhya*) are all subsumed under the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*)—namely, the grasping at "I" (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at names and conventions (*nāma-saṃketa-grāha*). The treatise states: "Both" refers to the seeds of karma;

"both the seeds of the two types of grasping" means that these proximate and remote conditions mutually assist one another. "The preceding maturation" refers to the karmic maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*) of successive prior lives. The remainder...
Regarding "ripening" (*vipāka*): it refers to subsequent births, which are the ripened fruits of karma.
Because the seeds of karma that induce further lives ripen, when the previous ripened fruit has been fully experienced, they are again able to produce other distinct ripened fruits.
It is by this means that the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) revolves without end; why then rely on external conditions for its continuity?

If there is only consciousness, for what reason does the World-Honored One, in various sūtras, speak of the three natures? One should know that the three natures, too, are not separate from consciousness.
"If there is only consciousness" reiterates the correct principle of Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātra; "for what reason" below is the interrogative phrase. It should...

"Knowing that the three natures are also not separate from consciousness" is the answer. That the three natures are not separate from consciousness serves to reveal the correct principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Why is this so? The verse says:
Through various forms of conceptual construction, one constructs various things; this nature of being conceptually constructed is non-existent.

The dependent nature arises from conditions through discrimination, while the perfected nature is that which is eternally devoid of the former nature within it. Therefore, this [perfected nature] and the dependent [nature]—
Neither different nor not different, like the nature of impermanence and so forth; it is not that this is not seen.

This answers the meaning of the previous question, clarifying that the three natures are fundamentally not separate from consciousness, yet possess three names. The preceding four lines [express this].

This explains the nature of the pervasive imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The first phrase clarifies the mind that performs the imagination; the second phrase clarifies the objects that are imagined.

The third and fourth phrases clarify that the intrinsic natures of both the subject and the object are neither truly existent. The treatise states: It is called "pervasive imagination" because it imagines and calculates everywhere.
Because its categories are manifold, it is referred to as "this and that. This refers to the false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that performs the pervasive imagination.

That is to say, by means of various false conceptualizations, one universally imagines various objects of imagination—namely, the falsely grasped aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, whether as phenomena (*dharma*) or as a self (*ātman*), including their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa*).

This falsely grasped intrinsic nature and its specific characteristics are collectively termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Such a nature does not exist at all; this is the principle.

This is because, when one investigates through reasoning, [the object] cannot be apprehended. The verse states: "The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is that which arises from conditions through conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
