This explains the dependent nature: all things arise from conceptualization as their condition.

All mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) produced by various conditions, as well as the objective and subjective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*), whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), are all dependently originated, for they rely upon various conditions.
Because it can arise, the verse states that the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) exists "in relation to those" within the four alternatives. This explains the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*:

it is called "perfected" (*pariniṣpanna*) because it is the complete and perfect accomplishment of the true nature of all phenomena. This indicates that it is omnipresent and eternal, and its essence is not false or erroneous.
This *pariniṣpanna* exists upon that *paratantra* (dependent nature), being free from the false imaginings of the *parikalpita* (imagined nature). Furthermore, and...
The nature manifested by the illusion-like dependent [nature] is called the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Therefore, this perfected reality and the dependent arising are neither different nor non-different.
If they were different, this *tathatā* of perfected reality would not be the true nature of that dependent arising. If they were not different, then the perfected reality would be...

If it were impermanent, then both [the perfected nature and the dependent nature] would equally be pure objects; consequently, there would be no distinction between the functions of fundamental wisdom and subsequently attained wisdom.

This is because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the pure object of fundamental wisdom, whereas the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the impure object of subsequently attained wisdom.
The verse states, "like the nature of impermanence and so forth," which serves as an analogy for the aforementioned [point].

The meaning of being neither different nor non-different. The treatise says: For example, regarding such phenomena as impermanence and selflessness, if the nature of impermanence and so forth were different from the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) themselves, then those phenomena would not be impermanent and so forth.
If they were not different, then this [nature] would not be their common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

That is to say, form, mind, and other conditioned phenomena each possess their own distinct substance, which is called their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); yet they all equally belong to [the categories of] impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.

The absence of self and so forth are called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). If these two characteristics were different, then those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*) would not belong to impermanence and the rest.
If they were not different, then this nature of impermanence and so forth would not be the common characteristic of all phenomena.

For that which is called "common" is such that impermanence itself is impermanent, and conditioned phenomena themselves are conditioned phenomena; only in this way is the meaning of "common" revealed. The verse says: "It is not that one does not perceive this."
That [which is referred to] is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita*); that [other] is the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
This means that one must first perceive the perfected nature and realize the imagined nature, and only then can the dependent nature be known to be like an illusion. The treatise states:
"It is not possible to see that dependent nature without seeing this perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-tathatā*), nor without having realized that the imagined nature is empty."
Because one knows the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as it truly is, after non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) has realized suchness (tathatā),
one is only then able, within subsequently attained wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna), to fully comprehend the dependent nature as being like illusory phenomena and the like.
If there are three natures, how is it that the Blessed One taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature?
If there are three natures, this refers to the establishment of the meaning of the three self-natures as not being separate from consciousness-only in the Mahāyāna.
The phrase "How [is it] below? is an interrogative term; it means: since there are already three natures, how is it that the Blessed One taught that all phenomena...
Are they without intrinsic nature?
The verse says:
"Based precisely upon these three natures, those three absences of intrinsic nature are established; therefore, the Buddha spoke with intentional meaning."
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature: first, they lack the nature of characteristics; next, they lack an inherent nature;
and finally, they are devoid of the nature of the self and phenomena as they are grasped.
This ultimate truth of all phenomena is also suchness, for it is eternally as it is; it is the very reality of consciousness-only.

The first four lines directly answer the intent of the question. That is to say, when the Buddha speaks of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), he establishes those three kinds of non-nature based upon these three natures—namely, the imagined (*parikalpita*) and so forth. Therefore, the World-Honored Buddha spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the term "intentional meaning," it means that his underlying intention is concealed; there is merely the verbal expression [without revealing the full depth]. In the middle...

The four lines explain the establishment of the meaning of the three natures of non-existence (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). The first refers to the characteristic of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*), which is ultimately non-existent;

thus, the first nature of non-existence is established. Next, regarding the dependent (*paratantra*), because it lacks the inherent nature of external objects as imagined, the absence of an inherent nature is established.
Finally, regarding the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*), which is remote from both the dependent and the thoroughly imagined, the ultimate non-existence is established.
Regarding "nature" (*svabhāva*): it is further said that "by being far removed from the former" refers to being free from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

"being far removed from the imagined" (*parikalpita*) refers to being free from the imagined nature. The term "nature" indicates the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The final four lines explain the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*).
Regarding this "ultimate meaning of all phenomena" (*dharmāṇām paramārtha*): this term refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Because the perfected nature is the ultimate meaning among all phenomena, it is also suchness (*tathatā*). If it is eternally as the perfected nature, being able to remain far removed from the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*), it is the true nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*).

Next are five verses on the practice and stages of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). The treatise says: "Regarding the characteristics and nature of Consciousness-Only thus established, who enters it, through how many stages, and in what manner?"

Thus, below [the text] concludes the preceding explanation of the three types of transformation (*pariṇāma*), as well as the various phenomena such as the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), which are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Furthermore, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena, such as *tathatā* (suchness), is the nature (*svabhāva*) of consciousness-only. Who, below...?

This is precisely the inquiry: regarding what kind of person, within how many stages, and in what manner they awaken to and enter into the characteristics and nature of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

That is to say, one who possesses the two kinds of Mahāyāna lineage (*gotra*): first, the innate lineage (*prakṛtistha-gotra*), which has been inherent since beginningless time and is dependent upon...
The fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) contains, by its very nature, the seeds that serve as the cause for untainted dharmas; these are the two types of lineage formed through cultivation.

That is to say, having heard the dharmas that flow from the dharma-realm, one possesses both lineages—such as those consisting of hearing and so forth—and it is only by relying upon the five stages that one is able to attain realization.
This answers the first type of question regarding the nature of the lineage (*gotra*). "Nature" (*prakṛti*) here should be understood as "clan" (*jāti*).
A "clan" refers to a category. If there is an original essence, it is because one abides in the clan of the bodhisattva category.
If there is no original essence, it is because hearing the Mahāyāna teachings perfumes [the mind] to form the Mahāyāna clan. Therefore, it is called the "outflow of the dharmadhātu."
What are the five stages? First is the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), which refers to cultivating the Mahāyāna factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).
Based on the characteristics and nature of consciousness, one is able to develop profound faith and understanding. What are its characteristics? The verse says:

"Until consciousness has arisen, one seeks to abide in the nature of representation-only; yet one is still unable to suppress and extinguish the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two types of grasping.
From this point downward, the characteristics of the five stages, such as the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*), are clarified, providing a general answer to the second and third questions.
...as well. What is meant by "inferior"? This is clarified through a question and answer regarding the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).

Within this stage, one is able to have deep faith and understanding that the characteristics and nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) are neither defiled nor pure. The first two lines of the verse explain the boundaries of the stage of equipment;

that is, from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) until the time when the preparatory application (*prayoga*) has not yet arisen, it is called the stage of equipment. The latter two lines explain [the practice] within this stage.

Regarding "meritorious practice" (*guṅxing*): it refers to this stage wherein, although one desires to realize the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), one lacks the functional capacity to suppress and eliminate the two types of grasping (*dvaya-graha*).

By "two types of grasping," one means the grasping of verbal designations (*nāma-graha*) and the grasping of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha-graha*); these are precisely the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), namely the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The treatise states: "From the generation of the profound and firm mind of great enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) until the point when the [mental states] conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) have not yet arisen..."

Consciousness seeks to abide in the true ultimate nature of *vijñapti-mātra*. Up to this point, all stages are subsumed within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), because one cultivates various superior provisions for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and because one diligently seeks liberation for the sake of sentient beings;
for these reasons, it is also called the "factor conducive to liberation" (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*). As for "unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment," it is the ultimate...
This refers to the ultimate fruit within the stages. Regarding "superior provisions," these are the two matters of merit and wisdom subsumed under the six perfections.
One cultivates these provisions in order to seek this fruit, both for the benefit of oneself and for the sake of sentient beings.

As for "diligently seeking liberation," the bodhisattva’s generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) differs from that of the two vehicles (*yāna*), which delight in solitary tranquility and seek to realize *nirvāṇa* for themselves alone. Now, this...
The Bodhisattva, relying on the fruit of liberation, subdues and severs the afflictions (*kleśa*) and enters the contemplation of self-emptiness (*ātma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Having already resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahā-citta*), they do so for the sake of delivering sentient beings. As for the "fruit of liberation," it is the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, because one realizes it through liberation from the afflictions.

Second is the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*). This refers to cultivating the Mahāyāna aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) while abiding in the stage of application, whereby one is able to gradually suppress and eliminate the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
What are its characteristics? The verse says:
To manifest before oneself even a slight object, claiming it to be the nature of consciousness-only—because there is something apprehended, one does not truly abide in consciousness-only.

[This concludes] the questions and answers clarifying the characteristics of practice in the stage of application (*prayoga*). This refers to that which can suppress and eliminate [the grasping at] the characteristics and nature of consciousness-only.

"Grasping at that which is grasped. These first two lines of the verse explain the mode of activity within this stage. "A small object" refers to the mind that observes with mental images (*sanimitta*).
If one asks whose consciousness-nature this mind is, the latter two lines refute [that notion]. The Treatise says:
First, during the initial incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), the Bodhisattva has well prepared the provisions of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna-saṃbhāra*) and followed the path of liberation.

Once the stage of liberation has been perfected, one cultivates further preparatory practices (*prayoga*) in order to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and abide in the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), thereby subduing and eliminating the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
These four—namely, *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgra-dharma*—are collectively termed the "Aids to Penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Because it accords with the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) that leads toward reality and is proximate to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is designated by the name "preparatory application" (*prayoga*).

It is not the preceding stage of equipment (*sambhāra*), as it lacks the sense of mere preparation. The initial attainment of the sun of wisdom and the precursor to the fire of the Path is called the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage.

As the signs of light increase further and the stage of investigation reaches its culmination, it is called the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) stage. Sealing what preceded and conforming to what follows, the cognition of the emptiness of the object of patience is called... [the stage of Patience].
Regarding the stage of patience (*kṣānti*): because this is the most excellent among the dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is called "the supreme worldly dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).

Regarding the stage of penetration (*prativedha*): this refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in which bodhisattvas abide; it is called the stage of penetration because they penetrate reality as it truly is.
What are its characteristics? The verse says:
When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in consciousness-only, because one is free from the characteristics of the two grasps.

The question and answer clarify the characteristics of the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*). That is to say, in the stage of thorough penetration, one penetrates as it truly is (*yathābhūtam*) the characteristic and nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*);
its essence is *tathatā* (suchness). The first two lines of the verse refer to the time when a bodhisattva attains the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*):
regarding the object of focus and non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), there is nothing to be apprehended in either case. The latter two lines refer to the bodhisattva’s attainment...
Regarding abiding in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) as the true nature (*tathatā*): because it is far removed from the dual characteristics of grasper and grasped. The treatise states:

"When a bodhisattva, with respect to the objects of cognition, possesses non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) such that nothing at all is apprehended, and because they do not grasp at the various signs of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), at that time they are said to truly abide in consciousness-only.
This true ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) is the realization of suchness (*tathatā*)."
Wisdom and suchness are equal and identical, for both are free from the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped.
These characteristics of the grasper and the grasped are both the mind of conceptualization and attainment, appearing as the proliferation of discursive elaboration (*prapañca*).

Fourth is the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). This refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in which bodhisattvas dwell. Within this stage of cultivation, they repeatedly practice the cultivation of seeing reality as it truly is.
What are its characteristics? The verse says:

Non-apprehension and inconceivability—this is supramundane wisdom. Because one abandons the two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

This question-and-answer section clarifies the characteristics of the practice of cultivation, namely the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*). It is as previously seen regarding consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Regarding the principle of repeated cultivation, "non-attainment" refers to the absence of an object of grasping (*grāhya*), which is termed "non-attainment," and the absence of a subject of grasping (*grāhaka*), which is termed "inconceivable. This is because the supramundane wise one has severed the mundane.
"Because of abandoning the two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*)" means that by severing the seeds of the two obstacles, one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
"Thereby one attains the transformation of the basis" means that one is able to realize the two kinds of fruits. The treatise says:

After the Bodhisattva has arisen from the preceding path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), in order to sever the remaining obstacles and realize the transformation of the basis, he repeatedly cultivates non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). This wisdom is far removed from...
Because there is neither the grasped nor the grasper, it is said to be "non-attainment" and "inconceivable.

This is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*lokottara-nirvikalpa-jñāna*). It is called "supramundane" because it severs the mundane. The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two graspings are the root of the mundane;

since only this [wisdom] can sever them, it alone receives this name. By cultivating this repeatedly, one abandons the two types of heaviness (*dausthulya*) and the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*); thus it is established.
It is called "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) because it can abandon those two types of coarseness; thereby, one is able to realize the vast transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

"Basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), for it serves as the support for both defiled and purified phenomena. "Defiled" refers to the false and pervasive imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
"purified" refers to the true perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). "Transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) refers to the relinquishing of these two portions.

It is transformed and attained. Through the repeated cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one eliminates the coarse latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the two obstacles within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

Consequently, one is able to transform and abandon the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and is able to transform and attain the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) within the dependent nature.
By transforming the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one attains great nirvāṇa; by transforming the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one realizes unsurpassed [enlightenment].
Awakening.

Fifth is the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), which refers to abiding in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Having emerged from obstructions, it is perfectly luminous;
throughout the exhaustion of the future, it transforms sentient beings. What are its characteristics? The verse says:
This is the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), inconceivable, virtuous, and eternal; it is the body of bliss and liberation, which the Great Muni names the Dharma.
Through this dialogue, the characteristics of the ultimate stage are clarified. That is to say, in the ultimate stage, the characteristics and nature of consciousness-only transcend the obstructions.

Perfectly luminous, he further transforms sentient beings so that they awaken to and enter into *vijñaptimātratā*. This initial term in the verse refers to the first two fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*):
the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). Furthermore, the latter three lines of the verse all manifest the various names for these two fruits.

Because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been eternally exhausted, it is called the "untainted realm. Because it transcends the paths of mind and speech, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*), as its nature is that of pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*). Moreover...

It is called "virtuous" because it has no end; it is called "permanent" because it is free from affliction; it is also called "blissful" because afflictions have been completely severed, which is termed the "body of liberation";
and it is called the "dharma-body" because it is forever free from the two obstacles. The treatise states:

One should know that the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) attained during the preceding stage of cultivation is precisely the characteristic of the ultimate stage. This refers to what precedes [it].

Second is the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). This is subsumed within the ultimate untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). All outflows (*āsrava*) are eternally exhausted, and there is no further increase of outflows.

Because its nature is pure, perfect, and luminous, it is called "untainted" (*anāsrava*). "Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "storehouse," for it contains within it boundless, rare, and great merits;
or it has the meaning of "cause," for it can produce the benefits of the five vehicles, both mundane and supramundane.
Because it is a matter of bliss, this fruit of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is also inconceivable, for it transcends the path of discursive thought and verbal expression.
It is also virtuous, because its nature is that of pure dharmas (śukla-dharma). It is also eternal, because it has no end.

It is also peaceful and blissful, because it is free from affliction. The two fruits of the transformation of the basis attained by the followers of the Two Vehicles merely involve the permanent departure from the afflictions.
Because there is no distinction between the obstructed and the supreme dharmas, it is simply called the *vimuktikāya* (body of liberation).

Because the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has accomplished the unsurpassed dharma of silence, he is named the Great Muni. The two fruits attained by this Honored Muni, which are forever free from the two obstacles, are also called the *dharmakāya*.
It consists of immeasurable and boundless great qualities of merit, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
Because it is that which is adorned.
This concludes the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti-kārikā* (The Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only), concerning the mind.
